about: Which READING an arriving payload gets — the question §scxml-B-2-8-1
answers and that every SCE script engine answers for itself.
The clause names four readings and orders them: key-value pairs become
named properties; otherwise JSON becomes the corresponding object;
otherwise, "if the Processor can interpret the content as a valid XML
document, it MUST create the corresponding DOM structure"; and then the
sentence that closes it — "Otherwise, the Processor MUST treat the content
as a space-normalized string literal".
That final sentence is the one this table exists for. A leading `<` is a
GUESS about which reading applies, not the reading itself, and six of the
eight engines treated the guess as the answer. Measured 2026-08-19, for a
payload that opens with `<` and is not a well-formed document:
C++ QuickJS      `undefined`, plus an ERROR log line
C++ Lua          nil
Rust Lua         nil
Go Lua           nil
Python Lua       the space-normalized string
Kotlin QuickJS   the space-normalized string
Kotlin Lua       the space-normalized string
C11 Lua          the space-normalized string, and never a DOM at all
Four answers to one clause, from one repository. It went unnoticed because
nothing sent such a payload: the W3C IRP suite's XML payloads are all
well-formed, and `xml_data_is_a_dom_tree` covers `<data>` rather than the
event path. Then the repository filled `_event.data` in at 192 raise sites
with messages that name the failing construct — `<assign> to detail
failed` — so every platform error opens with `<`, and three backends
delivered nil.
The 2026-08-17 round removed a fifth reading, `load("return " .. payload)`,
which ran the payload as the receiver's own source language. It was removed
from the engines that had a lane and left in the two that did not: the C++
Lua engine and the Kotlin Lua engine still answered 5 for a payload of
`2 + 3`. `an expression is text` below is that case, and it is decisive in
both languages at once — `2 + 3` evaluates to 5 in Lua and in ECMAScript
alike, so one payload asks every engine the same question.
Two spellings per case, for the same reason `dom_read_surface.json` beside
this file carries two: `source` is the author's ECMAScript, which the
engines that run ECMAScript evaluate as written, and `lua` is that
expression after the frontend has lowered it, which is all the Rust, Go,
Python and Kotlin-Lua bindings ever see. A per-backend copy of a table
drifts toward the backend that reads it; one table cannot.

cases.group: the XML reading — conditioned on the content BEING XML
cases.note: The rung that works. Kept beside the failing one so a repair cannot satisfy the clause by abandoning the DOM: an engine that answered the normalized string for both would pass the case below and fail this one.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — a valid XML document becomes the corresponding DOM structure

cases.note: Leading whitespace does not stop it being a document, so the guess has to look past it. Every engine already skips whitespace before testing for `<`; pinned so a repair that rewrites the guess keeps that.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — a valid XML document becomes the corresponding DOM structure

cases.group: the fall-through — the clause's last sentence
cases.note: The payload every platform error in this repository carries. It opens with `<` because it names the SCXML construct that failed, and it is not a document. Three engines answered nil or undefined here, which drops the message the raise site was written to send.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — otherwise the Processor MUST treat the content as a space-normalized string literal

cases.note: A document that is well-formed up to the point it is truncated. The parse gets further before failing, so an engine that only checks the first tag rather than the whole parse answers differently here than above.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — otherwise the Processor MUST treat the content as a space-normalized string literal

cases.note: A lone `<` — the guess's shortest possible input, and the one a naive fall-through built on "strip the tags" turns into the empty string.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — otherwise the Processor MUST treat the content as a space-normalized string literal

cases.group: the JSON reading — the rung <send> writes to
cases.note: §scxml-B-2-9 serializes data leaving the data model to JSON, so this is the wire every backend's sender now uses. A regression here empties `_event.data` for every document, which is why it is asked beside the repair rather than left to the sender's own tests.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — JSON content becomes the corresponding object

cases.note: The same payload read for its string member, so a decoder that produced numbers and dropped strings cannot pass on the case above alone.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — JSON content becomes the corresponding object

cases.group: the string reading — text is text
cases.note: Space normalization is a READING, not a passthrough: pinned so "the payload was not evaluated" cannot be satisfied by handing the bytes over untouched.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — otherwise the Processor MUST treat the content as a space-normalized string literal

cases.note: An expression is text. Decisive in both languages at once — `2 + 3` evaluates to 5 in Lua and in ECMAScript alike — so this one payload asks every engine whether it reads the field or runs it. The C++ Lua and Kotlin Lua engines answered 5 until 2026-08-19; their four siblings had the same rung removed on 2026-08-17.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — otherwise the Processor MUST treat the content as a space-normalized string literal

cases.note: A payload that is a CALL in Lua. For the four Lua engines it asks the sharper half of the case above — reading it gives back its own text, running it gives back `x` and, on the way, sets `breached` in the session's own globals. For the ECMAScript engines it is simply text that is neither JSON nor XML, so it pins the same clause there for a different reason. The side effect itself is asked per engine, where the language is known.
cases.clause: §scxml-B-2-8-1 — otherwise the Processor MUST treat the content as a space-normalized string literal
